entries.title: Beware the New AI-Fueled Ransomware Boom
entries.summary: Fully automated ransomware hasn’t arrived—yet. But seemingly unsophisticated attackers are using AI tools to wreak havoc.
entries.content:
Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

With so much going on all the time, you may not have thought about ransomware and data extortion attacks in a minute, even though they’ve been among the the biggest cybersecurity threats to institutions—and, by extension, people—over the past decade. But in the new era of AI-powered and automated cyberattacks, the danger posed by ransomware is only increasing as cybercriminals profit by combining established methods with new techniques made possible or more accessible by AI.

It is difficult to determine exact numbers of ransomware attacks, given that victims don’t always disclose incidents and attackers wildly inflate their claims. But researchers who specialize in tracking and attempting to de-duplicate the field agree that claimed incidents have spiked over the last few months. Some put the number of alleged ransomware attacks on leak sites—where groups post alleged victims—at nearly 3,000 attacks over the summer. This would mean a 20 to 40 percent increase since the spring by some estimates. And, crucially, researchers emphasize that while volume always fluctuates somewhat, ransomware attacks overall have been consistently and concerningly elevated in recent years.

“What we see is most of the recent increase was fueled by international attacks; the United States was a little more steady, but still high, still a lot of attacks,” says Cynthia Kaiser, former FBI cyber deputy director who now leads research for the anti-ransomware platform Halcyon. “Internationally we’re seeing a lot more attacks. That to me is the really new part, and I do think it is in part fueled by AI.”

Fully AI-powered ransomware attacks have yet to emerge, perhaps because the criminal business model already works so effectively. But cybercriminals do appear to be using LLMs for some of the more mundane aspects of their attacks.

“We are seeing AI relied on more heavily in certain aspects of the ransomware attack chain, such as creating better phishing emails and in the negotiation process, but the ‘successful’ ransomware groups are still largely human operated,” says Allan Liska, a longtime ransomware researcher and threat intelligence analyst at Recorded Future. “But the fact that these groups are experimenting heavily with AI means that this could change going forward, and change quickly.”

Kaiser notes that broader trends in scamming are always relevant to ransomware, because attackers often use the same types of phishing and social engineering techniques to gain initial access to targeted systems. In Japan, for example, successful scamming has spiked drastically in recent months as AI enables foreign attackers to generate consistently convincing content in Japanese for the first time.

A few ransomware groups—namely, the Gentlemen, Qilin, and Akira—have emerged as some of the most prominent and stable operations in recent months. However, in their shadow is a range of smaller groups, emerging actors, and fragmentation of the ransomware ecosystem. In recent weeks, multiple new ransomware groups have appeared and quickly claimed to have attacked dozens of businesses. Halycon’s analysis says around 111 ransomware groups made claims of attacks between July and September this year.

One new group calling itself Global Secret Group claimed attacks on 48 victims, with more than half of these being listed on the same day, according to security firm ReliaQuest’s analysis. Another, called Storm, listed 71 victims in just 20 days. Not all of the attacks may be legitimate, but they still cause uncertainty for businesses.

“That growth has all happened because, in my eyes, this acceleration that AI has provided to these threat actors, essentially allowing for them to go out and start their own groups,” says Brandon Tirado, the director of threat research at ReliaQuest.

Instead of being beholden to traditional “ransomware-as-a-service” providers, all of the researchers Kernel Panic spoke to say they have seen more lone-wolf operators branching out. Tirado says his team recently managed to identify who is behind one new group and found that it is being run by an inexperienced teenager who has made more than $800,000 in under two weeks. He declined to name the teen publicly.

Halcyon’s Kaiser agrees that more actors are using AI to attempt to strike out on their own with expanded capabilities to trick targets, exploit vulnerabilities, check their code, and even compromise other groups’ remote-access tools to gain redundant access to a victim in case one avenue gets blocked. But she adds that it’s still not clear how successful these upstarts will be long-term. She suspects that many of them may surge initially and then burn out, because they don’t have the institutional knowledge and expanded resources of an established group.

While established attackers typically conduct “double extortion” attacks in which they deploy traditional ransomware that encrypts a victim’s systems while also exfiltrating a target’s data and then threatening to publish it online, those operating independently may be more likely to focus solely on data extortion to simplify their operations.

“The number of attacks that Recorded Future has seen this year already dwarfs the total number for 2025,” Liska says, “but the number of attacks involving encryption may actually decrease year over year.”

Spotted something we should include next week? Let us know at [email protected]. And stay safe out there.

entries.title: I Put the Best Digital Notebooks to the Test. Here Are My Favorites (2026)
entries.summary: These nifty tools combine the ease of jotting notes by hand with the power of saving them digitally.
entries.content:
Featured in this article

Do you take a lot of notes? Whether it's daily to-do lists, notes for class, or just jotting down thoughts, I've found the best digital notebooks to keep them organized. Sure, you could just open your Notes app, but physically writing something down helps you remember and learn more. Plus, I just love to write things down, and these digital notebooks keep me from burning through paper or losing a great idea I wrote down.

Most of these tablets use E Ink technology to give you a more paperlike experience to write your ideas and notes on. It's easy on the eyes and helps keep you distraction-free as you take your notes as a classic notebook would. As our team's resident obsessive notetaker, I've tried almost every digital notebook on the market to find the best ones worth buying. Whether you want to be able to take detailed notes and access them on your laptop, annotate a book, or have near-never-ending battery life, I've found a digital notebook for you. They're especially great for students who need to do a lot of note-taking and stay engaged without getting distracted by notifications and other apps.

If your notes need an upgrade, I highly recommend giving these a try. If you're looking for more organizational tools and e-paper gadgets, don't miss my guides to the Best Paper Planners, Best Digital Wall Calendars, and Best E-Readers That Aren't a Kindle.

Updated November 2026: The Supernote Manta is now our runner-up pick, and the Supernote Nomad is now our budget pick.

Comparing Our Favorite Digital Notebooks

Our Favorite Smart Pens

Neo Smartpen M1+ for $129: If you don't want an entire tablet to write your digitized notes on, you can get a smart pen to use on regular paper that will log your notes into its companion app. The Neo Smartpen M1+ was the thinnest and lightest smart pen former WIRED reviewer Medea Giordiano tried, and she easily used it with notebooks and planners alike. You'll pair it with the Neo Studio app, which has a notebook system that's easy to navigate and organize your notes.

Neo Smartpen Dimo for $59: This is the cheapest smart pen option and uses replaceable batteries. It isn't compatible with Google Calendar, iCal, or Outlook like our other picks.

Honorable Mentions

Boox Note Air4 C for $470: If you're looking for something a little more powerful than just taking notes and annotating, but still want the E Ink screen experience, then a Boox device is what you need. The Boox Note Air4 C has an e-paper screen and is primarily described as an “e-paper notebook,” but runs on Android 13 and has access to the Google Play Store, giving it more of a tablet feel that happens to have a colorful e-paper screen instead of your usual brightly lit iPad or Android tablet. You're able to easily access the web (called NeoBrowser) right from the Boox homepage, which usually takes several steps and is incredibly slow on a true digital notebook. You'll also access apps that look like a tablet, including an image gallery, calendar, music player, and tools like a clock, recorder, and calculator. It was a pick in this guide, but it's now out of stock for US warehouses (you can still order from the Hong Kong warehouse, but you might have to pay extra tariffs and fees), and there's a new version out, the Note Air5 ($530).

Kindle Scribe Colorsoft for $630 and Kindle Scribe (3rd Gen) for $500 and Kindle Scribe Without Front Light for $430: The new versions of the Kindle Scribe are still solid all-around devices that have a good mix of e-reader and digital notebook features, but I still prefer the older model's price point. While the new Scribe Colorsoft is a nice option if you want color, I think these are too expensive for what they are. The price comes from all the AI features packed into the device, plus connectivity to services like Google and Microsoft, but it still isn't as powerful as a ReMarkable or Supernote if you want better tools. My picks above are a better price for similar features, though the Scribe does have the most impressive battery life of any digital notebook device I've tried (and that's still true for the older model that I recommend above, too, so you don't need the newest model for the best battery life).

Moleskine Smart Writing Set for $225: Moleskine is already known for its notebooks, and the brand has a smart version now, too. Our team previously tested a version in 2018 that only cost $149, but the current version that's $224 is next on my list to test. The set comes with a notebook and pen that will pair with the Moleskine Notes app to show you your notes.

Montblanc Digital Paper for $950: Yes, that Montblanc, the one with the famous pens, now has a digital notebook of its own. It's no surprise that I'd call its digital pen one of the best. It's got a super-lightweight feel while sporting three different buttons, two of which you can customize. (There's no eraser, but I'll give it up for that end of the pen to instead be a home button). I really like this device overall, but it's pricey for what you get—aside from the customizable pen buttons, there's not much to differentiate it from my top picks.

ReMarkable Paper Pro Move for $449: The ReMarkable Paper Pro Move is similar in size to a reporter's notebook, which turns out to be a pretty great size for daily task and to-do lists. There's room for a multilevel to-do list and brainstorming, and it's a nice, small size with just a 7.3-inch screen. There are other small options on the market, but this is the only one designed like a long notebook rather than a square, e-reader-like design. I like this size to layer on top of a paper planner or slip into a bag. It can do everything the larger Paper Pro can, including packing a color screen, and honestly feels like you sliced off a bottom third of the device and kept using it.

ReMarkable Paper Pure for $399: This is another good budget option if you want something larger than the Supernote Nomad. It has the same price as the second-generation Kindle Scribe I adore, but with more powerful digital notebook tools instead of a focus on reading. If you're looking for a great digital notebook without spending the better part of a grand, ReMarkable's new Paper Pure is its new basic digital notebook with a black-and-white screen, a lightweight feel, and a great writing experience that is one of the closest things you'll get to writing on actual paper. It doesn't have a front light, though, so you need to use it in lit rooms only.

ReMarkable 2 for $419 (Refurbished): This is the older ReMarkable digital notebook from 2020, and it's still a great device with a great range of accessories—while they're still available, that is. This device is only available refurbished or secondhand after getting essentially replaced earlier this year with the ReMarkable Paper Pure.

Rocketbook Fusion Plus for $30: If you really prefer the paper experience and don't want something you need to charge, then Rocketbook is for you. Rocketbook makes several reusable notebooks, planners, and accessories like index cards and sticky notes. I like the Rocketbook Fusion Plus since it comes with a ton of different template styles, from your classic monthly and weekly pages to project management layouts and meeting notes, making it feel closer to the variety a digital notebook can offer you. Take notes with an erasable Pilot Frixion Pen (one comes with whichever item you buy), scan photos of the pages into the Rocketbook app, and erase the whole thing with the damp microfiber cloth (also included). The app is designed to keep everything organized and easily send things off to Google Drive, Slack, Trello, OneNote, and a handful of other options.

FAQs

Do You Need a Digital Note-Taking Device?

The short answer is no. These devices are expensive, usually costing several hundred dollars when a simple notebook and pen costs a few bucks. But if you like the physical act of writing but need to have digital copies, they're worth considering.

Pros:

  • Digital notebooks are thin and light but hold hundreds of notes.
  • You can transcribe your notes into text files, making them easier to read and manipulate.
  • Depending on the device, you can export files as PDFs, Google Docs, Evernote files, and more.
  • Instantly digitizes your art, too.

Cons:

  • Expensive.
  • Need to be charged.
  • Have a learning curve.
  • Most smart pens need to be paired with an accompanying notebook. The upcoming Nuwa Pen promises smart notes on any paper.

What About an iPad?

E Ink notebooks are easier on the eyes and feel closer to paper than a glass-screened tablet. But in some cases, you might spend less getting an iPad and an Apple Pencil (and a keyboard if you also want to type sometimes). You can also do more on them thanks to the thousands of apps in the App Store. An iPad is pretty intuitive if you're familiar with the Apple ecosystem (though both ReMarkable and Supernote's ecosystems are also very intuitive). Past WIRED reviewers liked using an iPad with the GoodNotes and Notability apps; check out our guide to the Best iPads for more advice on which to buy.

I also have an iPad, and I'll say the upside of a digital notebook is that the battery tends to last longer, especially if you're the type to use it for a day or two and then forget about it for a few days. My trusty Kindle Scribe usually manages to have plenty of battery available for whenever I feel the note-taking itch, even if it's been a week or two since I last touched it.

Why Are Digital Notebooks So Expensive?

Just because these devices look like paper doesn't mean they're as cheap to make as a sheet of paper. Like any tablet or smartphone, these devices are packed with features, a special ecosystem, and the E Ink technology is no small feat to perfect, along with a sensation similar to writing on paper. It's an impressive piece of technology.

Prices haven't gotten cheaper for this category in the wake of tariffs' causing technology prices to rise. ReMarkable recently raised the price of our top pick, the ReMarkable Paper Pro. Another favorite of ours from Supernote has gone up a little less than $50, and Kobo also slightly raised its prices, though the $10 increase is pretty minor compared to other increases we’ve seen. We'll continue to monitor prices and flag if more price changes are to come.

entries.title: How to Run SteamOS on Your Mac
entries.summary: A free app lets you boot SteamOS in a virtual machine on your Apple Silicon Mac, unlocking PC and legacy games that otherwise won’t run.
entries.content:
Most of my Steam collection won't run on my Mac. It's not (entirely) my fault.

I will be the first to admit that my collection is mostly old indie games, all of which work fine on Windows. Less so on the Mac. Apple stopped supporting 32-bit games back in 2019 when it released macOS Catalina. A good chunk of my Steam library has a "No" symbol next to it because of that restriction. And next year it will get even worse: macOS will drop support for running Intel Mac applications, which could leave even more games unplayable (though Apple claims that certain older games will keep working).

But there's another way. A free, open source app called FX Steam Launcher boots the ARM version of SteamOS—the operating system that powers Valve's Steam Deck gaming handheld—right on your Mac, using a combination of a virtual machine and compatibility layers. You will need a Mac with an Apple Silicon processor, as Intel Macs aren't supported, running macOS 15 or later. I set this up recently, connected a controller, and I've been playing all kinds of games that are otherwise unplayable on my MacBook Air.

It wasn't even hard to set up. To get started, download the application, mount the DMG file, and drag the app to your Applications folder. The first time you launch the application, a pop-up will offer to download and install SteamOS for you in a virtual machine.

Click Create New Disk, and you'll be asked a few questions. The most important step is the hard drive size—the default is 64 GB, which is plenty, but consider allocating more space if you plan on installing multiple large games. You can also choose the drive location, if you like, and set a password for opening SteamOS.

Click Create, and the application will download SteamOS and install it in a virtual machine. I recommend using this time to pair a game controller with your Mac in System Settings under Bluetooth. FX Steam Launcher works with most current gamepads, including Xbox, DualSense, DualShock, and Made for iPhone. I used a Nintendo Pro Controller.

Eventually, you will see the login screen, where you can enter your Steam credentials. Once you're in, you'll see your Steam library. The virtual machine operates like an actual Steam Deck, which takes some getting used to if you've never used one. It divides your library into games known to work in SteamOS and those that might work, which is helpful. A lot of my games started running immediately, with full gamepad support.

This isn't a drop-in solution for every game. SteamOS itself is quite fiddly, and you're now running it in a virtual machine. In some cases, I needed to tweak the graphics settings for games to run correctly. For Psychonauts, specifically, I had to download a user-made patch to get the controller working properly—but I'd have needed that fix for an actual Steam Deck too. When a game ran poorly, I frequently found the solution by Googling and finding actual Steam Deck owners who ran into similar problems.

There is a limit to the processing power you get out of a Mac, especially if you (like me) are using a MacBook Air. And a virtual machine, by definition, doesn't have access to all of your machine's capabilities. But the list of compatible games, compiled from other users, shows which devices have successfully played various titles. Check that page for your favorite games before you dive in.

If nothing else, this is a lot easier than my previous method for running Windows games on a Mac, which involved setting up a version of Wine that's no longer supported. I even got a few non-Steam games installed. Sideloading on SteamOS means booting into Desktop Mode, which you can find in the SteamOS sidebar under Power. You'll end up in a Linux-based desktop, complete with a web browser. You can download games, put them in the folder of your choice, and point Steam to them. I couldn't add custom art, but I got multiple games up and running this way.

Honestly, Valve should update the official Steam Mac client with similar compatibility tech so it can run Windows games natively. It would be a huge hit with Mac users.

If you're a power user, I recommend checking out the settings for FX Steam Launcher, which you can open from the menu bar or with the keyboard shortcut Command-comma. You can change the resolution for your virtual Steam Deck, configure the sound to your liking, and submit game statistics.

It's remarkable software. And, with an HDMI cable and a gamepad, you can plug your MacBook into your TV and game from your couch. That's what I plan on doing when I'm done writing this article (which I guess is right now).

entries.title: It’s Time to Run an Audit of All the Cloud Storage Links You’ve Shared
entries.summary: Those old links you shared with friends ages ago are still live, and they might be attracting unwelcome visitors.
entries.content:
Cloud storage certainly has a lot going for it. For a start, if you drop your laptop into the sink, it's likely that a lot of your important work will be backed up somewhere in the cloud, as long as you’re using services such as Google Drive, OneDrive, and iCloud.

Then there's file sharing: Not too many years ago, swapping large amounts of data with other people meant dragging and dropping and running around with USB drives (and perhaps even mailing them). Now, via a couple of clicks and a link, you can share just about anything with just about anyone, anywhere in the world.

However, this comes with security risks attached. You don't want those links making their way to anyone they weren't intended for, otherwise they've got access to your files and folders. They could potentially see what's in them, and maybe even make changes or delete files, depending on the permissions you've set.

It's worth emphasizing that sharing files through these cloud storage services isn't inherently insecure—these shared links are actually very well protected, by default. However, the longer they stick around, the bigger the risk gets. Your links could get mistakenly forwarded in an email, or one of your contacts could have their email account hacked.

With that in mind it's prudent to run a regular audit on the cloud sharing links you've got active. It shouldn't take long: The apps involved usually make this pretty straightforward. Once you've closed a link down, no one else can get to it.

Microsoft OneDrive

If you head to the Microsoft OneDrive portal on the web, you'll see a Shared link in the navigation pane on the left: Click this, then select By you up at the top of the file list to see everything you've shared with other people. Use the Modified header if you want to sort the files and folders by the oldest or most recent.

Click the three dots next to any file or folder, then Manage access to control who can get to it. If you've shared the file with specific people, you can remove some or all of them; if the file or folder is shared more widely with just a link, clicking the trash can gets rid of it. You can also open up Office files to manage access there.

It's worth knowing that when you opt to share a file in OneDrive on the web (via the three dots and Share), if you click the cog icon on the Share panel you can set an expiration date for the sharing—which saves you the trouble of having to tidy it up afterwards.

Apple iCloud

If iCloud Drive is your cloud storage service of choice, once you've got the main interface up on the web, you can click Shared on the navigation pane on the left to go straight to the files and folders you're sharing with other people. There's no easy way to sort them, but you can use the search box up in the top right corner.

Click the three dots next to a file and folder, then Managed Shared File, to make changes. The next screen lets you block access for specific contacts, and to change permissions (from editing to just viewing, for example). If you want to cancel the sharing altogether, click Stop sharing.

Unlike OneDrive, iCloud doesn't give you any way of putting expiration periods on shared links, so you have to clear them up manually.

Dropbox

Dropbox is one of the more aggressive services when it comes to tidying up shared links, and if you use the Dropbox apps you might see reminders to review the files and folders you've shared with others. From Dropbox on the web, click Shared in the left-hand navigation pane to see files and folders you're currently sharing.

You can get quite a detailed breakdown here, including by Files or by Folders. Click the three dots next to any entry, then Share, to see the current sharing options: You can remove access for contacts one by one, or click the cog icon (top left) to find the Unshare button that ends all sharing completely.

Dropbox does have link expiry features built in: If you open up the share settings whenever you're sharing a file or folder, you'll see Link expiry is one of the options. It's an easy way to tidy up after yourself, provided the people you're sharing the file or folder with get around to viewing it in time.

Google Drive

Google Drive, surprisingly, isn't quite as on top of shared links as other cloud storage services. If you open up the web portal, there's no easy to access list of everything you've shared: The closest thing to it is clicking the People filter, and then choosing contacts to see files and folders you've shared with them specifically. If you pick Anyone with the link from the drop-down list, you'll see everything shared with a simple link.

To change the sharing settings for a file or folder, click on the three dots, then Share. Click the cog icon on the panel that pops up, then you can remove contacts as needed and turn the visible link off.

As with iCloud, there's no link expiry feature you can rely on here, so shared files and folders can't be set to become unshared after a certain time has elapsed. It has to be done manually, so it's a shame Google doesn't make it as easy as it could be.

entries.title: 10 Best Early Black Friday Headphone Deals (2026): Up to 50% Off
entries.summary: Get up to 50 percent off some of my favorite headphones and earbuds from Apple, Sony, Nothing, and more.
entries.content:
Right now is a great time to buy a new pair of headphones. Brands have largely finished launching their latest models for the year, leaving some great discounts on older generations. As part of early Black Friday deals, I'm even seeing some of the latest and greatest models on sale for the first time. I've been reviewing headphones for more than four years, and I'm currently eyeing the 50-percent-off deals on older Sony headphones in particular.

All the deals below are WIRED-tested products we stand by, including wireless earbuds and over-ear headphones. For more early Black Friday deals, check out our guides to the Best Early Black Friday TV Deals and the Best Early Black Friday Mattress Deals.

Updated November 14: I added new products on sale from Nothing, CMF, and Shokz, and removed products no longer on sale from Bose, Google, and Beats.

Best Earbud Deals

Apple AirPods Pro 3 are the best wireless earbuds not only for anyone with an iPhone—but also for anyone who wants to keep things simple. They sound great and have some of the best active-noise-canceling (ANC) and transparency modes on the market. They also seamlessly sync with all of your Apple devices. While 20 percent off isn't the best price I've seen for them, it's still a solid discount.

The Nothing Ear (3a) are one of our favorite pairs of earbuds under $100, and 30 percent off is the biggest discount I've ever seen for them so far. They have a semi-transparent design and bold colors that stand out from the crowd (particularly the yellow version). While the automated noise-canceling isn't the best, it's hard to fault them at this new low price.

The Shokz OpenFit open ear headphones were one of my favorites before the newer clip-on open earbud design started becoming more popular. This is the lowest price I've ever seen the Shokz model go for. They wrap around the top and back of your ear and rest there, leaving your inner ear clear to hear the outside world around you. The OpenFit 2+ have great sound quality (for open ear headphones, that is), long battery life, and wireless charging support.

Best Over-Ear Headphone Deals

The more premium XM6 and the newly revived, cheaper XM4C have effectively replaced the Sony WH-1000XM5. But I am still seeing the blue colorway of these excellent headphones at the lowest price I've clocked for these sunsetting cans. When they launched in 2022, they were our top pick for over-ear headphones. They remain excellent and far outperform other options at this limited price.

The Nothing Headphone (1) are a home run in looks and sound, and they are at their lowest price ever ahead of Black Friday. They’re solid noise cancelers with a bold, transparent design on the ear cups that's somehow techy, retro, and futuristic-looking. Among their best features are the on-ear controls, namely the clicky wheel that adjusts volume and the flat rocker paddle that you can push back and forth to move to the previous track or skip ahead, respectively.

The budget Nothing Headphone (a) and premium Nothing Headphone (1) Pro are also on sale, but the Headphone (1) is the most appealing deal in my view.

Sony recently launched the WH-CN730N to replace these headphones, hence the rock-bottom price of 50 percent off. While these headphones can't compete with most specs of more premium options on this list, they're ultra-lightweight at just 192 grams. That and 35 hours of battery life with ANC on is nothing to scoff at.

Want to spend even less on headphones? CMF is Nothing's sub-brand focused on stylish designs at a lower price point, and this is the best deal I've seen on its Headphone Pro over-ear cans. Frankly, $49 is a steal for these headphones, considering they are comfortable, sound surprisingly good, and have noise-canceling and long battery life.

Want the best ANC over-ear headphones? Look no further than the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (2nd Gen). They are the benchmark to which I compare other ANC headphones. Plus, they are comfortable, premium, and sound excellent.

My top over-ear headphone pick, the best-in-class Sony WH-1000XM6 is matching the lowest price I've seen. These headphones are amazing across the board, with their high comfort, superior sound quality, and great noise-canceling capability.

AirPods Max 2 are excellent over-ear headphones for Apple fans, but the $550 sticker price is frankly absurd. Thankfully, they are almost always a little bit on sale, including now. This is far from the best deal I've seen on these headphones, and I do expect the price to dip further during Black Friday sales events, so I would add them to my cart and wait to pull the trigger.
